messages.subject: Multivariate t distribution
parts:
Hello all,

I was just wondering whether there are plans yet to implement a multivariate t distribution in Stan? (If I am correct in thinking that it currently isn't implemented?)

If not, are there any work-arounds that you might suggest?

Best,

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Multivariate t distribution
parts:
On Wednesday, August 5, 2015 at 10:31:46 AM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
I was just wondering whether there are plans yet to implement a multivariate t distribution in Stan? (If I am correct in thinking that it currently isn't implemented?)
It is there (or at least one of them is), is called multi_student_t.
If not, are there any work-arounds that you might suggest?

Even though multi_student_t exists, you should only use if for a likelihood of data. For an unknown, it is better to express a multivariate t random variable as a mixture of normals as in

http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-2/hofert.pdf

Ben

Equation 3, where A is a Cholesky factor of the dispersion matrix for the multivariate t distribution. In other words, iid standard normal priors on the elements of Z and a scaled inverse chi-squared prior on W implies a multivariate student t prior on X with mode mu and dispersion matrix A * A'.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Multivariate t distribution
parts:
On Wednesday, August 5, 2015 at 1:07:46 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
Ok - that makes sense. Again being dense - why is this better than just using:

theta ~ multi_student_t(nu,mu,Sigma);

Is it because this actually produces a random variable which is described by equation (8)?

No. It has to do with the posterior geometry. For small values of nu, the elements of theta have long tails and a lot of tail dependence. If theta were something declared in the parameters block, then it would be very difficult and perhaps impossible for Stan to find a stepsize that would allow it to efficiently sample from both the tails and the mode. If you utilize the stochastic representation, then the prior distribution of Z and W has no dependence and moderate tails, so Stan will obtain an effective sample size that is very close to the nominal sample size.

But, your .stan program is not quite right:

transformed data {
   matrix[n,n] A;

    A <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
}

You need a parameters block like

parameters{
  real<lower=0> W;
  vector[n] Z;
}

in which case W should not be declared in the transformed parameters block

transformed parameters {
  real W; // eliminate this
  vector[n] theta;

  W <- nu/W_denom; // and this
  theta <-  mu + sqrt(W) * A * Z; // keep this
}

This is not good either:

model {
W_denom ~ chi_square(nu);
Z ~ multi_normal(rep(0,n), Identity_matrix);
}

Never use a multi_normal with a diagonal covariance matrix; just use independent univariate normals. Also, there is a scaled_inv_chi_square distribution built into Stan. So, it could just be

model {
  W ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(nu);
  Z ~ normal(0,1);
}

Ben
